es.summary: La ERGE es una condición crónica en la que el contenido gástrico regresa al esófago, provocando irritación y síntomas como pirosis. Puede derivar en complicaciones estructurales si no se controla.
key_points: Diagnóstico clínico basado en síntomas ≥ 2 veces/semana o evidencia endoscópica.
Modificaciones de estilo de vida son la primera línea de tratamiento.
Los inhibidores de la bomba de protones son la terapia farmacológica de elección.
Complicaciones incluyen esofagitis, estenosis y esófago de Barrett.

pathophysiology: El esfínter esofágico inferior (EEI) se relaja inapropiadamente o tiene presión basal baja.
El contenido ácido del estómago retrocede al esófago, dañando la mucosa escamosa.
La lesión crónica estimula reparación y proliferación de células progenitoras, pudiendo generar metaplasia (Barrett).
risk_factors: Obesidad y aumento de presión intraabdominal.
Embarazo (presión del útero y relajación hormonal).
Alimentos grasos, chocolate, cafeína, menta y comidas copiosas.
signs_symptoms: Pirosis o sensación de ardor retroesternal, especialmente después de comer.
Regurgitación de contenido ácido al cuello o boca.
Disfagia o odinofagia en casos de esofagitis.
diagnostics: Endoscopia digestiva alta: erosiones, esofagitis o Barrett.
pH-metría esofágica de 24 h: pH < 4 > 4 % del tiempo.
Radiografía con bario: reflujo y posible hernia hiatal.
Prueba de respuesta a inhibidor de bomba de protones (PPI) como diagnóstico empírico.
treatment: Modificaciones de estilo de vida: elevar cabecera, evitar comidas 2‑3 h antes de acostarse.
Antiácidos (hidróxido de aluminio/magnesio) para alivio rápido.
Antagonistas H2 (ranitidina, famotidina) para síntomas leves‑moderados.
Inhibidores de la bomba de protones (omeprazol, esomeprazol) como terapia de primera línea.
nursing_care: Evaluar dolor y pirosis usando escala de 0‑10 antes y después de comidas.
Monitorear signos de aspiración: tos, cambios en saturación O₂.
Registrar ingesta y horarios de alimentos; educar sobre porciones pequeñas y masticación adecuada.
Posicionar al paciente en decúbito lateral izquierdo o semi‑sentado 30‑60 min post‑prandial.
Reforzar adherencia a terapia farmacológica y cambios de estilo de vida.
patient_teaching: Evitar comidas grasosas, chocolate, cafeína y alcohol.
No acostarse dentro de 2‑3 h después de comer; elevar cabecera de la cama.
Perder peso si tiene sobrepeso; usar ropa suelta.
Tomar los medicamentos según indicación, sin omitir dosis.
Reportar síntomas de sangrado (hematemesis) o pérdida de peso inexplicada.

outcomes: Sin evidencia de aspiración: ausencia de tos durante y después de las comidas

interventions.action: Mantener al paciente en posición semi‑sentada (30‑45°) durante y al menos 30 min después de comer
interventions.rationale: Reduce el reflujo y el riesgo de que el contenido gástrico sea aspirado

interventions.action: Evaluar signos de aspiración (tos, cambios en auscultación, saturación) cada 4 h
interventions.rationale: Detección temprana permite intervención rápida

interventions.action: Enseñar al paciente a masticar bien y comer porciones pequeñas
interventions.rationale: Disminuye la presión intraabdominal y el volumen de contenido gástrico

interventions.action: Reforzar la adherencia a inhibidores de bomba de protones según prescripción
interventions.rationale: Controla la acidez y reduce la irritación del esófago

interventions.action: Registrar cualquier episodio de regurgitación o tos durante la alimentación
interventions.rationale: Proporciona datos para evaluar la efectividad de las intervenciones

evidenced_by: queja de fatiga al realizar actividades después de comer
disminución de la tolerancia al ejercicio
outcomes: Realizar caminata de 15 min sin dolor ni pirosis
Nivel de energía ≥ 7/10 en escala de 0‑10

interventions.action: Planificar comidas pequeñas y frecuentes cada 3‑4 h
interventions.rationale: Reduce la carga gástrica y la probabilidad de síntomas durante la actividad

interventions.action: Programar actividades físicas de baja intensidad después de 2 h de la última comida
interventions.rationale: Permite vaciamiento gástrico antes del ejercicio

interventions.action: Enseñar técnicas de respiración diafragmática para aliviar la pirosis
interventions.rationale: Mejora la presión intraabdominal y reduce el reflujo

interventions.action: Monitorear nivel de dolor y pirosis antes, durante y después de la actividad
interventions.rationale: Facilita ajustes en el plan de ejercicio y medicación

interventions.rationale: Optimiza el control de la enfermedad y mejora la tolerancia a la actividad

en.summary: GERD is a chronic condition in which gastric contents return to the esophagus, causing irritation and symptoms such as heartburn. It can lead to structural complications if not controlled.
key_points: Clinical diagnosis based on symptoms ≥2 times/week or endoscopic evidence.
Proton pump inhibitors are the preferred pharmacologic therapy.
Complications include esophagitis, strictures, and Barrett’s esophagus.

pathophysiology: The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxes inappropriately or has low basal pressure.
Acidic gastric content refluxes into the esophagus, damaging the squamous mucosa.
Chronic injury stimulates repair and proliferation of progenitor cells, potentially leading to metaplasia (Barrett).
risk_factors: High-fat foods, chocolate, caffeine, mint, and large meals.
signs_symptoms: Heartburn or retrosternal burning sensation, especially after eating.
Regurgitation of acidic content to the neck or mouth.
Dysphagia or odynophagia in cases of esophagitis.
diagnostics: Upper endoscopy: erosions, esophagitis, or Barrett’s.
24‑hour esophageal pH monitoring: pH < 4 > 4 % of the time.
Barium swallow: reflux and possible hiatal hernia.
PPI response test as empirical diagnosis.
treatment: Lifestyle modifications: elevate head of bed, avoid meals 2‑3 h before bedtime.
H2 antagonists (ranitidine, famotidine) for mild‑moderate symptoms.
Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, esomeprazole) as first‑line therapy.
nursing_care: Assess pain and heartburn using a 0‑10 scale before and after meals.
Monitor for aspiration signs: cough, changes in O₂ saturation.
Record intake and meal times; educate on small portions and adequate chewing.
Position patient in left lateral or semi‑upright 30‑60 min post‑meal.
Reinforce medication adherence and lifestyle changes.
patient_teaching: Avoid fatty foods, chocolate, caffeine, and alcohol.
Do not lie down within 2‑3 h after eating; elevate head of bed.
Lose weight if overweight; wear loose clothing.
Take medications as prescribed, do not skip doses.
Report bleeding symptoms (hematemesis) or unexplained weight loss.

outcomes: No evidence of aspiration: absence of cough during and after meals

interventions.action: Keep patient in semi‑upright (30‑45°) position during and at least 30 min after meals
interventions.rationale: Reduces reflux and risk of gastric content aspiration

interventions.action: Assess for aspiration signs (cough, auscultation changes, saturation) every 4 h
interventions.rationale: Early detection allows prompt intervention

interventions.action: Teach patient to chew well and eat small portions
interventions.rationale: Decreases intraabdominal pressure and gastric volume

interventions.action: Reinforce adherence to prescribed proton pump inhibitors
interventions.rationale: Controls acidity and reduces esophageal irritation

interventions.action: Document any regurgitation or cough episodes during feeding
interventions.rationale: Provides data to evaluate intervention effectiveness

evidenced_by: complaint of fatigue during activities after meals
outcomes: Walk 15 min without pain or heartburn

interventions.action: Plan small, frequent meals every 3‑4 h
interventions.rationale: Reduces gastric load and symptom likelihood during activity

interventions.action: Schedule low‑intensity physical activity after 2 h from last meal
interventions.rationale: Allows gastric emptying before exercise

interventions.action: Teach diaphragmatic breathing techniques to relieve heartburn
interventions.rationale: Improves intraabdominal pressure and reduces reflux

interventions.action: Monitor pain and heartburn before, during, and after activity
interventions.rationale: Facilitates adjustments to exercise plan and medication

interventions.action: Coordinate with physician to adjust pharmacologic therapy if symptoms persist
interventions.rationale: Optimizes disease control and improves activity tolerance

summary.0.quote: GERD is a chronic (long-lasting) condition that can cause discomfort and, over time, lead to other health problems.

summary.1.quote: GERD is a chronic (long-lasting) condition that can cause discomfort and, over time, lead to other health problems.

key_points.3.quote: If not treated, GERD can cause problems like inflammation of the esophagus , scar

sections.pathophysiology.0.quote: GERD can happen when the muscle at the bottom of your esophagus becomes weak or relaxes at the wrong time.

sections.pathophysiology.2.quote: The continuous damage and wound healing causes progenitor cells (cells that can differentiate into a specific cell type) from the esophagogastric junction to travel to the esophagus to aid in wound healing and replace the squamous epithelial cells.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: You are more likely to have GERD if you: Are overweight or have obesity Are pregnant Smoke or are around secondhand smoke Have a hiatal hernia (when part of the stomach pushes up into the chest) Certain foods, drinks, or medicines can also make GERD worse.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: You are more likely to have GERD if you: Are overweight or have obesity Are pregnant Smoke or are around secondhand smoke Have a hiatal hernia (when part of the stomach pushes up into the chest) Certain foods, drinks, or medicines can also make GERD worse.

sections.risk_factors.3.quote: Acute gastritis is usually caused by an irritant, such as aspirin or NSAID use, heavy alcohol use, smoking, and certain infections.

sections.risk_factors.4.quote: Avoiding foods that trigger symptoms, such as spicy foods, chocolate, caffeine, or fatty foods

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: The most common symptom of GERD is heartburn . This is a burning feeling in your chest or throat.

sections.signs_symptoms.1.quote: Stomach contents can then move back up and irritate the esophagus.

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: In some cases, Barrett’s esophagus can cause ulceration and stricture, and patients may have the symptoms of dysphagia or odynophagia (painful swallowing).

sections.signs_symptoms.3.quote: It can also worsen asthma or cause chronic (long-term) cough or hoarseness.

sections.diagnostics.2.quote: An upper GI series, or barium swallow, can check for GERD, dysphagia , hiatal hernia, ulcers, tumors, or achalasia.

sections.treatment.0.quote: Lifestyle changes can include: Eating smaller meals and avoiding lying down for at least 2-3 hours after eating Avoiding foods that trigger symptoms, such as spicy foods, chocolate, caffeine, or fatty foods Losing weight if needed Raising the head of your bed Quitting smoking

sections.complications.0.quote: Raberprazole GERD Peptic and esophageal ulcers Erosive esophagitis H. pylori infection Zollinger-Ellison syndrome May cause kidney damage Can interfere with the liver metabolism of other drugs Long-term therapy can cause hypomagnesemia.

sections.complications.2.quote: A condition called Barrett’s esophagus entails the cells lining the esophagus change, becoming more like intestinal cells.

sections.complications.3.quote: The cells that develop on the esophagus can be precancerous and increase the patient’s chance of developing esophageal adenocarcinoma (Souza & Spechler, 2022).

sections.nursing_care.4.quote: Most people can manage GERD with lifestyle changes and medicine.

sections.patient_teaching.0.quote: Foods that are spicy, fatty, acidic, or contain caffeine, carbonation, or alcohol can exacerbate symptoms of reflux and heartburn and trigger episodes of odynophagia or dysphagia.

sections.patient_teaching.1.quote: Eating smaller meals and avoiding lying down for at least 2-3 hours after eating Avoiding foods that trigger symptoms, such as spicy foods, chocolate, caffeine, or fatty foods Losing weight if needed Raising the head of your bed Quitting smoking

sections.patient_teaching.2.quote: You may be able to improve symptoms of GERD by: Avoiding alcohol and trigger foods Eating smaller meals Not eating close to bedtime Wearing loose-fitting clothes Sleeping on your left side or raising the head of your bed Maintaining a healthy weight

sections.patient_teaching.4.quote: For PUD, life-threatening, or alarm symptoms that warrant immediate action are bleeding or anemia early satiety family history of GI cancers progressive dysphagia or odynophagia recurrent vomiting unexplained weight loss
